<reason>Both sides were sharp and disciplined. CON built a genuinely dangerous dilemma (privacy or portability, never both) and an original reframe (the graph belongs to everyone in it), and it forced PRO to concede that mutual ties need acceptance. But PRO answered the pressure more convincingly: it leaned on the motion's own word "interoperable" to argue the leaver stays reachable without bulk-copying anyone, which is a legitimate reading of the proposition rather than a rewrite; CON's late move to declare that portability means only a one-time copy and that federation is off-motion was the weaker interpretive position. PRO also extracted and exploited concessions—CON admitted lock-in is "not acceptable," offered "bans on blocking exports" (a portability mandate minus the standard), and its MySpace/Digg examples were turned into proof of the coordination problem PRO described from the start. CON's compelled-carriage and persistent-ID costs remained partly live, keeping this competitive, but PRO made the comparison (conceded structural exit failure vs. design risks that a federated standard can mitigate) easier to decide.</reason>
<best_rebuttal>The exchange over B2.3's dilemma and A4.1–A4.3's interoperability answer: CON's "first mover lands alone" attack was the debate's strongest pressure, but PRO's reply that interoperability means the leaver stays reachable (email/number portability never required everyone to move) blunted it, and CON's counter that this "rewrites the motion" conceded too much ground on the plain text.</best_rebuttal>
